summary: This experimental RFC extends OLSRv2, a routing protocol for wireless mesh networks, so one network can maintain several separate routing topologies at once. It stays interoperable with OLSRv2 routers that do not support the extension. It also updates RFC 7188 and RFC 7631 by changing their TLV registries and descriptions.

plainLanguage.summary: OLSRv2 is a routing protocol for wireless networks where the computers move around. It normally keeps one set of routes, all measured the same way. This RFC lets a router keep several sets of routes at once, each measured differently, and still work with older routers that know only one way to measure.

subtitle: How OLSRv2 wireless mesh routers can keep one routing table per link metric while staying compatible with plain OLSRv2.

tldr.problem: OLSRv2 uses a single link metric type for all of its routes, so a wireless mesh network cannot route different traffic over different measures of link quality.
tldr.mechanism: Each router picks a set of link metric types per interface, advertises them in a new MPR_TYPES TLV, and keeps a separate Routing Set, MPR calculation and willingness value for every type.
tldr.outcome: Routers that do not implement the extension still work in the same network, because the first metric type in every message is always the one plain OLSRv2 uses.

today: RFC 7722 is an Experimental RFC that updates RFC 7188 and RFC 7631, and no RFC obsoletes it. The document was published to collect experimental experience, with the intent of proposing the extension for the Standards Track once that evidence exists.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (RFC 7181, OLSRv2) is a proactive link state routing protocol designed for use in Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs), where computers move around and connect to each other without fixed infrastructure. One of the improvements of OLSRv2 over its experimental precursor is the ability to use link metrics to select routes other than minimum hop routes.

The limitation this document addresses is that OLSRv2 uses a single link metric type for all routes. In some MANETs it would be desirable to route packets using more than one link metric type. The extension described here permits that while maintaining maximal interoperability with OLSRv2 routers that do not implement it.

The purpose of OLSRv2 can be described as creating and maintaining a Routing Set, which holds everything needed to fill an IP routing table. In the same way, the role of this extension is to create and maintain multiple Routing Sets, one for each link metric type the router supports.

Multi-topology routing is a natural extension to a link state routing protocol such as OSPF, but it does not yet benefit from extensive operational or even experimental experience for OLSRv2. The document is published to collect that experience, with the intent that an OLSRv2 Multi-Topology Routing Extension will be proposed for the Standards Track once suitable evidence exists. Experiments are encouraged, especially reports covering mixed networks, dynamic topologies, realistic deployments, which link metric types proved useful, and the resource requirements of running the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: OLSRv2 is a routing protocol for wireless networks where the computers move around. It normally keeps one set of routes, all measured the same way. This RFC lets a router keep several sets of routes at once, each measured differently, and still work with older routers that know only one way to measure.

sections.title: Applicability and Interoperability
sections.content:
The extension applies to any MANET where OLSRv2 is otherwise applicable, but in which several topologies are maintained, each characterized by a different choice of link metric type. It is assumed, but outside the scope of this document, that the network layer can choose which topology to use for each packet, for example by using the Diffserv Code Point (DSCP) defined in RFC 2474.

That selection of topology MUST be consistent: each router receiving a packet must make the same choice of link metric type, so that each packet uses a single topology. This is necessary to avoid the possibility of a packet looping in the network.

A MANET can contain both routers that implement this extension and routers that do not, and that do not know it exists. Where non-extended routers may be present, the single link metric used by those routers must be included in the set of link metrics for each interface of an extended router that may hear them. The extension does not modify the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol that OLSRv2 builds on, and does not use or modify its link quality mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router has to agree which set of routes a given packet should follow. If two routers disagree, the packet could travel in circles. Routers that do not know about the extension can still be part of the same network.

sections.title: Parameters and Information Bases
sections.content:
The single router parameter LINK_METRIC_TYPE used by routers that do not implement the extension is replaced by an interface parameter array IFACE_METRIC_TYPES and a router parameter array ROUTER_METRIC_TYPES, the union of all interface arrays. Each element of these arrays is a link metric type, that is, a Type Extension of the LINK_METRIC TLV. Both arrays MUST be without repetitions. Where non-extended routers might exist, LINK_METRIC_TYPE MUST be the first element of both arrays, and ROUTER_METRIC_TYPES MUST also include it first. The router parameter WILL_ROUTING is extended to an array of values, one for each link metric type in ROUTER_METRIC_TYPES.

In the information bases, many single values become maps from a set of metric types to their values. The values are a boolean, a willingness (a 4-bit unsigned integer from 0 to 15), a number of hops (an 8-bit unsigned integer from 0 to 255), or a link metric. Link and neighbour metrics are held per interface metric type, while neighbour willingness, routing MPR status, MPR selector status and advertised status, and the router, routable address and attached network metrics are held per router metric type.

There is a separate Routing Set for each link metric type in ROUTER_METRIC_TYPES. A Routing Set is calculated as in RFC 7181, except that where an element is now a map, the value for the selected link metric type is used, and a protocol tuple whose link metric is UNKNOWN_METRIC is ignored for that calculation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps a list of the kinds of measurement it supports, and a separate set of routes for each kind. Measurements it knows nothing about are simply skipped.

sections.title: New and Extended TLVs
sections.content:
A new MPR_TYPES message TLV is defined with the same Type as the MPR_WILLING TLV but with Type Extension 1, so that its presence signals that the router supports the extension in the same way that the presence of MPR_WILLING signals support for OLSRv2. A message MUST NOT contain more than one of them. Its Value field carries one octet per supported link metric type, on the sending interface for a HELLO message and on any interface for a TC message. Where non-extended routers might exist, the first octet MUST be LINK_METRIC_TYPE.

The MPR_WILLING TLV value is extended with additional 4-bit sub-fields for willingness to act as a routing MPR, one per link metric type, ordered as reported in the MPR_TYPES TLV. If the number of metric types is even, the unused 4-bit sub-field in the last octet SHOULD be cleared on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. A value field shorter than full length is read as missing willingness values of zero, WILL_NEVER, which is how an OLSRv2 router that does not implement the extension avoids acting as a routing MPR for a metric it does not recognize.

The LINK_METRIC TLV is unchanged, but its Type Extension range is extended from 0 to the range 0-7. The MPR TLV value becomes a variable-length bitfield: one bit for flooding status and one bit for routing MPR status for each link metric type, in the order given by the MPR_TYPES TLV. The two least significant bits of the first octet keep the value that a router without the extension would produce. The GATEWAY TLV value may also become variable-length, carrying one octet of hop count per link metric type, with the first octet holding the value a router without the extension would produce.

HELLO and TC message processing is extended accordingly. If a message carries an MPR_TYPES TLV whose first metric type is not LINK_METRIC_TYPE, and non-extended routers might exist, the message MUST be silently discarded. Metric types supported only by the receiving router are set to their defaults: UNKNOWN_METRIC, WILL_NEVER or false.

For IANA, this document modifies Message TLV Type 7 by changing the description of the MPR_WILLING Type Extension and adding the MPR_TYPES Type Extension, and it replaces the tables for the MPR TLV bit values, the GATEWAY TLV and the LINK_METRIC TLV allocations. Type Extensions 0-7 of the LINK_METRIC TLV are assigned by administrative action, 8-223 remain for Expert Review and 224-255 for Experimental Use.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message now says which kinds of measurement the sender supports, in a fixed order. The first one is always the kind that older routers understand, so they can still read the start of the message. A message that starts with the wrong kind is thrown away.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
A network using the extension usually needs more management than one using unmodified OLSRv2, and the use of multiple metric types across the MANET has to be managed by administrative configuration or otherwise. A bad collective choice of metric types will make the MANET anywhere from inefficient to nonfunctional.

Four decisions are called out. First, deciding which link metric, and hence which Routing Set, to use for received packets. All routers MUST make the same decision for the same packet, and an obvious approach is to map each DSCP to a single link metric. Second, selecting which link metrics to support on each interface, since different interfaces may have different physical and data link properties. Third, ensuring that the MANET is sufficiently connected, for example by ensuring that sufficiently many routers implement each metric type needed. If any routers might not implement the extension, the MANET will be connected to the maximum extent possible using LINK_METRIC_TYPE, but that will only serve to deliver packets that use that metric type.

Fourth, routers that do not implement the extension SHOULD be managed so as not to produce packets that will be routed by a topology they are not part of. Should that happen, such a packet is routed until it reaches its destination or reaches an extended router, where it is either dropped or routed by that topology. Such a packet will not loop. A packet created for a destination outside the corresponding topology may or may not be delivered if the originating router is a non-extended router, and will not be sent if the originating router is an extended router.

The meanings of link metric types are at the discretion of the MANET operator. They could represent packets of different types, packets in streams of different rates, or packets with different trust requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone has to decide which set of routes each kind of packet uses, and make sure enough routers know each set. Otherwise some packets may not arrive, or may arrive the long way round.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension lets a router support more than one link metric type for each link advertised in HELLO and TC messages, and lets routers support different sets of types. Link metric values of additional types are reported by including additional TLVs in the messages, which report known values of all supported types.

HELLO and TC message processing is then extended simply to record, for each supported type, all of the received link metric values for each link. Protocol-internal processing, specifically MPR set and shortest path calculations, then operates as specified in RFC 7181 for each link metric type that the router supports.

Consequently the security considerations of RFC 7181, including its security architecture and mandatory security mechanisms, apply directly. The extension introduces no additional vulnerabilities beyond those of RFC 7181, because each link metric type is used independently, and each one could have been the single link metric type supported by an implementation of RFC 7181 receiving the same information, since received information of an unsupported type is ignored by all routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules stay the same as in plain OLSRv2. Each kind of measurement is used on its own, so an extra kind cannot weaken the protection of the others.

items.title: Link and neighbour metric values
items.text: The measured cost of the link in each direction, one value per metric type.

items.text: Whether this neighbour was selected to relay routes for this metric type.

items.text: Whether this neighbour says it will act as a routing MPR.

items.title: Advertised neighbour status
items.text: Whether the neighbour's own routing information has been received.
